title: The Adjustment Bureau
full_review:
With its unusual blend of the ordinary and the supernatural, not to mention its "Mad Men"-era costuming, "The Adjustment Bureau" (Universal) might suitably be subtitled "The Angel in the Gray Flannel Suit."

Of course, writer-director George Nolfi's script for this curious drama -- adapted from Philip K. Dick's 1954 short story "Adjustment Team" -- plays predictably coy when it comes to pinning down the exact identity of these dapper characters and the precise origins of their superhuman powers. Asked directly about the A-word, for instance, one of them replies, "We've been called that."

But, presuming they do hail from the choirs celestial, as opposed to being mere aliens or something else entirely, we may at last have the answer to a question no scholastic philosopher of the Middle Ages ever thought to ask: "Do angels look good in fedoras?"

And just what, you wonder, are these retro-chic denizens of a hidden world (played, principally, by Anthony Mackie, John Slattery -- best known for his role on the aforementioned "Mad Men" -- and Terence Stamp) doing in contemporary Manhattan?

As the officials of an invisible bureaucracy to end all bureaucracies, they're intent on breaking up the budding relationship between promising youthful politician David Norris (Matt Damon) and gifted dancer Elise Sellas (Emily Blunt). The success of the couple's courtship -- which was never supposed to get started in the first place -- would, it seems, run contrary to the predetermined plans of an unnamed higher power.

Having been informed of all this -- as well as of the dire consequences of trying to thwart the workings of destiny -- David reluctantly but abruptly walks out on Elise. But fortune, which can't seem to make up its mind, eventually brings the pair back together again.

With its ambitious pitting of love against fate -- or perhaps against divine providence -- Nolfi's feature debut will intrigue some viewers, even as it strikes others as an uneasy attempt to blend science fiction, romance and philosophical speculation.

Though this is certainly not a film for young people -- in addition to the quasi-theological issues underlying the story, David and Elise's liaison becomes physical prematurely -- the metaphysical elements of the plot can be interpreted by mature viewers in a way that squares with Judeo-Christian faith.

The film contains complex themes, brief nongraphic premarital sexual activity, a couple of uses of profanity and rough terms and considerable crude and crass language. The Catholic News Service classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
